title: M105, NGC 3379
caption: The elliptical galaxy M105 and neighbors in the Leo I group, imaged by the KPNO 0.9-meter telescope

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: Three galaxies share this frame. M105 is the one on the right, a smooth elliptical galaxy classed as type E1. Above and to the left of center is NGC 3384, another member of the same group, and at the bottom left sits a galaxy that lies far behind them in the background.

M105 is the brightest galaxy in the Leo I group, a gathering that also includes M95, M96 and a number of fainter galaxies. The whole group is about 40 million light-years away. Elliptical galaxies like M105 lack spiral arms and appear as soft, rounded glows of mostly older stars.

Its light fades so evenly from center to edge that astronomers once used M105 as a standard for measuring how brightness is spread across galaxies. Closer study later showed that it is not quite as smooth, or as standard, as first thought, which the caption notes is the usual fate of any galaxy examined closely enough.
scale: The Leo I group is about 40 million light-years away, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: A CCD camera on the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak recorded these galaxies in visible light, and the frames were combined into a color composite. The color mapping is not published.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures gather far more light than the eye, bringing out the extended glow of all three galaxies.

explore: This CCD color composite was taken with the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory on 5 February 1996 (Universal Time). Every picture of M105 includes NGC 3384, because the two sit so close together on the sky.
alt: A smooth, rounded galaxy at right, a second galaxy above and left of center, and a smaller background galaxy at bottom left.
